reasoning: The core problem — whether prompting an LLM judge to resist/flag manipulation improves robustness — is substantially studied. "Can You Trick the Grader?" (EMNLP 2025 Findings) formalizes seven rhetorical manipulation techniques, embeds them into responses, and explicitly tests counter-prompting defenses, finding the persuasive effect persists under counter-prompting and that model size does not help — essentially the headline result this proposal would seek, though in math-answer scoring rather than QuALITY debate transcripts. The "Can We Trust the Judge?" protocol and related three-agent debate work add an explicit bias-estimator component that flags manipulative subclaims in debate, and Kenton et al. (NeurIPS 2024) is exactly the QuALITY weak-judge-vs-strong-debater setting; broader LLM-judge debiasing work finds prompt-only mitigation only partially reduces persuasion bias. What remains genuinely unexplored is the specific instantiation: a prompt-only "meta-judge" wrapper (list tactics -> flag manipulation -> score) applied to existing bias-exploiting QuALITY debate transcripts using small open weak judges and measuring truthful-side accuracy delta. The method/setting combination is novel, but the underlying problem and likely outcome are largely characterized, so the marginal contribution is incremental.

evidence.title: Can You Trick the Grader? Adversarial Persuasion of LLM Judges
evidence.summary: Formalizes seven rhetorical/persuasion techniques (Majority, Consistency, Flattery, Authority, etc.), embeds them in responses, and shows LLM judges inflate scores to incorrect answers by up to 8%. Crucially tests counter-prompting defenses and finds the persuasive effect persists under counter-prompting, with model size not mitigating it — directly pre-empts the proposal's prompt-only manipulation-aware defense, albeit in scoring rather than debate transcripts.

evidence.title: Can We Trust the Judge? A novel method of Modelling Human Bias and Systematic Error in Debate-Based Scalable Oversight
evidence.summary: Debate-based scalable-oversight protocol adding a bias-estimator agent ('Bob') that detects manipulative subclaims exploiting judge cognitive vulnerabilities — the same manipulation-flagging goal as the proposed meta-judge, but implemented as an extra agent rather than a prompt-only wrapper.

evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs
evidence.summary: Establishes the QuALITY weak-judge-vs-strong-debater experimental setting the proposal builds on; notes weak judges (e.g. Gemma7B) may be too weak to benefit and that natural-language persuasion by incorrect debaters reduces judge accuracy.

evidence.title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
evidence.summary: Foundational QuALITY debate work showing persuasion affects judge accuracy and that truthful-side win-rate is the key metric; the transcript corpus and accuracy metric the proposal reuses originate here.

evidence.title: Evaluating and Mitigating LLM-as-a-judge Bias / prompt-engineering mitigation findings
evidence.summary: Surveys/evaluates judge-bias mitigations and finds prompt engineering instructing models to ignore bias cues only partially reduces persuasion and fails against strong injections, supporting that a prompt-only meta-judge is likely to yield limited, already-anticipated gains.
